issues.legal_issue: A finding that reverses a trial court’s assessment of a witness is unsustainable when it relies on selected portions of the testimony and ignores material cross-examination without cogent reasons.
material_facts: The trial court considered the witness’s examination-in-chief and cross-examination and found his evidence unreliable as proof that the original tenancy authorized subletting.

The appellate authority relied on part of the witness’s examination-in-chief while disregarding material parts of his cross-examination, without giving cogent reasons for rejecting the trial court’s assessment.
The High Court, exercising rent-control revision jurisdiction, declined to accept the appellate authority’s finding.
issues.conclusion: The appellate authority’s finding was vitiated by misreading the testimony and was perverse; the High Court was right to disregard it and rely on the trial court’s assessment.
issues.legal_principle: A court must assess a witness’s whole testimony, including cross-examination, because cross-examination tests what was stated in examination-in-chief. A finding based on selected testimony while ignoring material parts may be perverse and unsustainable. Although revision under Section 20 of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965 does not generally permit reappraisal of evidence or substitution of the revisional court’s conclusion for that of the appellate authority, as stated in Ubaiba v. Damodaran, (1999) 5 SCC 645, that restriction does not protect a finding founded on misreading or omission of material evidence.

rule.if: rent_control_revision and trial_court_assessed_whole_testimony and appellate_authority_relied_on_selective_testimony and not appellate_authority_gave_cogent_reasons

predicates.rent_control_revision: The proceeding is a revision in a rent-control dispute.
predicates.trial_court_assessed_whole_testimony: The trial court evaluated the witness’s testimony as a whole, including cross-examination.
predicates.appellate_authority_relied_on_selective_: The appellate authority relied on selected testimony while disregarding material parts of the witness’s evidence.
predicates.appellate_authority_gave_cogent_reasons: The appellate authority gave cogent reasons for departing from the trial court’s assessment.
predicates.appellate_finding_is_perverse: The appellate authority’s finding is perverse and unsustainable.

issues.definition: In a rent-control revision, an appellate finding is perverse when it departs from the trial court’s assessment of whole testimony by relying selectively on it without cogent reasons.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s subletting without the landlord’s consent does not become authorized merely because the landlord knew of it, remained inactive, or accepted rent; consent requires positive and clear landlord action where the tenancy does not grant a right to sublet.
material_facts: The tenancy began before the rent-control statute came into force, and sublettings were made both before and after it came into force.
The tenant produced no reliable evidence that the landlord had affirmatively authorized the later sublettings or that the tenancy granted a right to sublet.
The landlord knew of the sublettings, did not object for some years, and accepted rent, but served notice seeking termination of the subletting arrangements.
The landlord sought eviction on the ground of unauthorized subletting under Section 11(4)(i) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s inaction and conduct did not establish implied consent or waiver. The tenant’s later sublettings, unsupported by positive consent or a tenancy right to sublet, justified eviction under Section 11(4)(i).
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(4)(i) of the Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965 permits recovery of possession where, after commencement of the Act, a tenant transfers lease rights or sublets without the landlord’s consent and the lease does not confer a right to do so. In this context, consent requires positive, clear action; mere silence, inaction, knowledge, or acceptance of rent is insufficient. The distinction between consent and acquiescence is supported by Bell v. Alfred Franks & Bartlett Co. Ltd., [1980] 1 All ER 356. Hiralal Kapur v. Prabhu Choudhury, AIR 1988 SC 852, and Ram Saran v. Pyare Lal, AIR 1996 SC 2361, support the conclusion that knowledge of another’s occupation or acceptance of rent does not by itself establish consent to subletting. Sublettings made before the Act commenced do not attract this statutory ground.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_for_subletting and subletting_after_governing_law_commenced and lease_does_not_authorize_subletting and not affirmative_landlord_consent

predicates.rent_control_eviction_for_subletting: The proceeding seeks eviction in a rent-control case on the ground that the tenant sublet or transferred the premises.
predicates.subletting_after_governing_law_commenced: The tenant sublet or transferred the premises after the governing rent-control law commenced.
predicates.lease_does_not_authorize_subletting: The tenancy does not grant the tenant a right to sublet or transfer the premises.
predicates.affirmative_landlord_consent: The landlord took positive action clearly consenting to the subletting or transfer.
predicates.eviction_available_for_unauthorized_subl: Eviction is available on the ground of unauthorized subletting or transfer.

issues.definition: When a rent-control eviction proceeding concerns post-commencement subletting, the lease grants no right to sublet, and the landlord did not affirmatively consent, eviction is available on that ground.
